# Present Research and Contributions

First, as highlighted above, a comprehensive evaluation of LSAM beyond bias and variability of point estimates was not previously feasible because analytical SEs had not been derived. To enable this, we developed and present an analytical formula for calculating SEs that accounts for the uncertainty of both estimation steps in the LSAM approach (see Appendix A).

Second, earlier simulation work comparing LMS, QML, and UPI was limited to commercial software or error-prone implementations with a slow estimation process [@kjell_etall_2024], and simulation designs lacked the ability to generate data with exact covariance control while also allowing for a non-normal copula. Recent developments in open-source software [@R-modsem] and data generation tools [@gronneberg_foldnes_2022] allow us to address these limitations, making this also the first simulation to be based solely on open-source implementations. We adopt a copula-based framework for data generation, which has been largely ignored in the literature, with the exception of @lonati_etall_2024, although their approach based on @mair_etall_2012 distorts both the marginal distributions and the copula structure when enforcing the target covariance matrix [@gronneberg_foldnes_2022].

Third, the literature often suggests that the LMS, QML, and UPI face "scalability" limitations as higher-order terms increase [@rosseel_etall_2025; @kelava_etall_2011], though the extent remains unclear. This may explain why previous literature focused on elementary interaction models (EIM) [@jaccard_wan_1995], with few studies examining models with up to three nonlinear terms (e.g., Klein & Muthen, 2007, Brandt et al., 2014). In fact, little work has addressed statistical models with multiple endogenous variables for LMS and QML [@jin_etall_2020], requiring specific programming modifications [@kjell_etall_2024]. However, researchers are fitting (or trying to fit) much more complex models in practice [@hamilton_etall_2024; @drum_etall_2017; @li_etall_2019]. To address this, we consider models with three and eight nonlinear effects among latent variables. We note, however, that LMS was excluded from the latter case due to computational constraints. This will be further discussed as it is related to the scalability issue.

Last, while some of simulation design factors (e.g., sample size and reliability) and performance metrics (e.g., coverage) considered here have been examined for some approaches, they have not been systematically investigated for others. These distinctions are clarified in the following sections.
